title_options: I Built a YouTube Factory With Claude That Runs While My Laptop Is Off
I Automated a YouTube Channel With Claude. Version 1 Was a Disaster.
My Laptop Was Off. This Video Still Made Itself.
thumbnail_prompt: Dark green cyber background, huge white text MY LAPTOP WAS OFF with OFF highlighted in green, glowing ring containing $0
seo_description:
I built a pipeline with Claude that turns a script file into a finished YouTube draft on a free cloud machine: neural voice, motion graphics, captions, a thumbnail and backups, all from one GitHub commit. This is the honest build log, including the first version that looked like AI slop, the bugs that nearly broke everything, and the YouTube monetization rule that changed how the whole system works.

You'll see the free stack (GitHub Actions, a neural text-to-speech library, Remotion, Google Drive and the YouTube Data API), what each piece costs, the research behind the topic (2,368 videos across 122 channels), and the limits I haven't solved yet.

The narration voice is synthetic. Every script is researched with AI and reviewed by a human before it's rendered.

scenes.narration: This video was produced by a pipeline I built with Claude. It rendered on a cloud computer, so my laptop could have been switched off the whole time. The first version was so bad it wouldn't have been eligible to earn a single cent. So here's exactly how it works, what broke, and what I changed.
scenes.chapter: Why I built a video robot

chart.title: One Script In, One Draft Out

steps.title: Write the script
steps.detail: Scenes, narration and charts as data

steps.title: Private draft
steps.detail: Waits in YouTube Studio for review

scenes.narration: The idea is simple. I write a script as a structured file, where every scene gets narration, a chart and a caption. I push that file to GitHub. A cloud computer wakes up, records a voice, animates the visuals and uploads a private draft. My job is the part a machine can't do: deciding what's worth saying.

Five pieces make this work, and every one is free to start. GitHub Actions provides the cloud computer. A neural text to speech library reads the script. Remotion turns React code into video frames. Google Drive keeps a backup of every file. And the YouTube API stages the finished video as a private draft for me to check.

chart.title: One Real Test Run, Measured
chart.subtitle: GitHub Actions job for a 46-second test video

scenes.narration: GitHub Actions is the engine. Every time a new script lands in the repository, it boots a fresh Ubuntu machine, installs FFmpeg, Node and Python, then runs my build script. When the job finishes, the machine is thrown away. Standard runners cost nothing on a public repository, which is why the render bill for this video is zero.

chart.title: cron — every Sunday 04:30 UTC
commands: > found the next episode in the queue

scenes.narration: There's also a schedule. Every Sunday at ten in the morning, India time, a timed job wakes the same machine without any commit at all. It checks Google Drive for scripts that haven't been rendered yet, picks the next one in each channel's queue, and builds it. If the queue is empty, it simply does nothing.

chart.title: tts — en-US-BrianNeural
commands: > recording when every word starts and ends

scenes.narration: The voice you're hearing is synthetic. It comes from a free neural text to speech library, and the clever part is the timing data. As it speaks, it reports exactly when each word starts and ends. That timing drives the captions under this sentence, highlighting every word in yellow at the moment it's spoken.

chart.title: Editing Software vs Video as Code
left_points: Clips dragged onto a timeline by hand
right_points: A cloud machine does the rendering

scenes.narration: The visuals are where it gets interesting. Remotion lets you describe a video in React, the same code used to build websites. Every chart, card and animation is a component, and a headless Chrome browser captures it thirty times per second. Claude wrote most of these components, and I reviewed and fixed what it got wrong.

chart.title: How Each Scene Is Sized
chart.subtitle: Rules every script has to follow

scenes.narration: Each scene is deliberately short. A scene holds between forty five and sixty five words of narration, which works out to roughly twenty seconds on screen. Then the visual changes. That rule exists because a viewer's attention drifts when the picture stays still, and a still picture is exactly what automated videos are known for.

chart.title: The First Test Video
chart.subtitle: What the very first render actually looked like

scenes.narration: Here's the uncomfortable part. The first test video was forty six seconds long, built from plain text cards sitting on a grid. It looked automated, because it was. If you've ever clicked on a faceless channel and left after five seconds, you already know exactly what it felt like to watch that first version.

When I looked closer, the problems stacked up. There was no thumbnail, so YouTube would pick a random frame. Under the voice sat a constant hum made from three sine waves, meant to pass as ambient music. And some charts showed numbers nobody had measured, which is the fastest way to lose a viewer's trust.

Then came the bugs. The most confusing one was a single line. When code was pasted between tools, a web address was quietly converted into a markdown link, brackets and all. The script still looked fine at a glance, but every login to Google would have failed, so no video could ever have reached Drive or YouTube.
scenes.chapter: The bugs nobody warns you about

chart.title: The Safety Net Every File Passes

steps.title: Commit
steps.detail: Only verified files reach the cloud

scenes.narration: Pasting caused a second problem. Long code files kept getting cut off around twenty kilobytes, and some lines arrived scrambled, with quotes in the wrong places. The fix was boring but essential. Every file is now type checked and test bundled before it's committed, so a broken paste can never reach the render machine.

chart.title: YouTube Data API: The Daily Budget
chart.subtitle: Default quota for a new Google Cloud project

scenes.narration: The third wall was a quota. To research which videos actually perform, I pulled data from YouTube's own API, and it shut me out halfway through. Free API access comes with a daily budget, and a single search costs a hundred units. The research only finished the next day, after the budget reset at midnight Pacific time.

chart.title: What YouTube Will and Won't Pay For

scenes.narration: The biggest lesson wasn't technical. YouTube won't pay channels for what it calls inauthentic content: videos that look mass produced from a template, with little variation and no real insight. Its reviewers judge the whole channel, not one upload. So a factory that stamps out identical videos is building a channel that can never earn.
scenes.chapter: The rule that kills most AI channels

chart.title: Automate the Labour, Keep the Judgement

scenes.narration: That changed how I think about automation. The machine should handle the parts that are pure labour: recording, animating, encoding and uploading. The parts that decide whether a video deserves to exist, picking the topic, checking the facts and adding a point of view, stay with a human. In this pipeline, that human is me.

chart.title: Before Writing a Single Word
chart.subtitle: Recent uploads from channels in the AI workflow niche

scenes.narration: So before writing this script, I did the research first. I pulled two thousand three hundred and sixty eight recent videos from a hundred and twenty two channels in the AI workflow niche. Then I ranked every video against its own channel's typical views, so a small channel's breakout counts as much as a big channel's normal day.

chart.title: Breakouts: Views vs the Channel's Own Median
chart.subtitle: Long-form uploads since May 2026

scenes.narration: The pattern was clear. The biggest breakout was a video about making a viral video using only Claude, at fifty one times its channel's usual views. Close behind were motion graphics with Claude and faceless shorts built with Claude. People don't just want AI news. They want to see the real workflow, mistakes included.

chart.title: remotion still — Thumbnail
commands: ✓ custom thumbnail set on the draft

scenes.narration: Next came packaging. Every video now gets a thumbnail generated by the same render engine: three or four huge words, one highlighted, high contrast, readable at the size of a phone search result. The pipeline uploads it with the video automatically, so nothing ships with a random frame ever again.

chart.title: Why Every Upload Starts Private
left_points: Bad uploads hurt the whole channel

scenes.narration: One rule never changes: nothing goes public on its own. Every upload lands as a private draft, already flagged to YouTube as containing synthetic media, because the voice is generated. I watch it, fix anything that slipped through, and press publish myself. Automation that publishes mistakes instantly is how channels get buried.

chart.title: How the Music Bed Is Mixed

scenes.narration: The sine wave hum is gone too. Now the pipeline pulls a royalty free instrumental track from a music folder, loops it well below the narration, and ducks it even further whenever the voice is speaking. It's a small change, but audio is usually the first thing that makes a video feel cheap.

chart.title: Who Did What on This Video

scenes.narration: Claude's role is worth being precise about. It wrote most of the rendering code, ran the research and drafted this script. It also caught several of my mistakes, including a title promising 4K when the pipeline actually renders 1080p. What it doesn't do is decide what this channel stands for. That part is still mine.

chart.title: The One Step I Refuse to Automate

scenes.narration: And the most important change is the slowest one. Every script, including this one, is drafted by Claude from real research, then reviewed by me before it's committed. I cut what's wrong, add what I actually think and check every number. Only then does the machine take over. It's the one step I refuse to automate.

chart.title: What This Pipeline Costs to Run

scenes.narration: So what does it actually cost? The cloud machine is free on a public repository. The voice library is free. Remotion is free for individuals and very small teams. Storage uses a Google Drive plan I already pay for. The real cost is time: writing, reviewing, and fixing whatever broke that week.

chart.title: The Honest Limits
chart.subtitle: Measured on GitHub's standard Linux runner

scenes.narration: There are limits. Rendering runs at roughly ten frames per second, so an eight minute video takes around twenty five minutes in the cloud. The free API budget caps how much research I can do each day. And the pipeline can't screen record yet, so it can't make click by click tutorials.
